general.statement: Products, brands, side projects, and artifacts from a lifetime of making things.
general.about:
My work spans digital product design, brand identity, and experience strategy, with a focus on getting new ventures off the ground.

Today, as a founding member at [Recidiviz](/p/a-civic-impact), I design catalytic systems that reduce the number of people incarcerated in the U.S. I established the initial team, our design standards, and the foundational product that made this mission scalable. Over our first four years, these efforts helped improve the living conditions of more than 100,000 people navigating the criminal justice system.

Previously, I ran an independent studio building brands and products for select clients. Before that, as a design lead at Google, I shaped the growth surfaces and city-scale programs that helped [Waze](/p/a-waze) double its user base to 110M MAUs, while also defining the [commuter experience](/p/a-smart-cities) for a broader smart-cities initiative within Area 120.

Outside of my career, you’ll find me reading esoteric essays, tinkering with cameras, or curating overly specific lists. Having spent my childhood in the Caribbean and my adolescence in California, I find rainy days beautifully nostalgic, but cold winters are my nemesis.

projects.heading: Civic Impact
projects.description:
Digital products aimed at systemic criminal justice issues in order to reduce the amount of people incarcerated in the U.S. Since 2019, I've worked on the product strategy, brand ethos, digital design system, website, and team operations.

As founding head of design, I stood up the design function and have hired and led the product design team as we grew from a single state partnership into a corrections platform used across more than twenty state partners. The work runs from data foundation through the tools staff use daily: stitching fragmented justice data into a shared layer, then designing the products that sit on top of it, including supervision and case-planning workflows.

When I established the design function, our core challenge was that justice data lived across disconnected databases, spreadsheets, and paper files. We grounded our product strategy in mapping the full human journey from intake through community integration. To support that journey, our team built tools on two fronts: staff-facing software that cuts busywork for officers, and tools for incarcerated people that let them track progress and act for themselves.

Over our first four years, this collective effort helped improve system navigation and living conditions for more than 100,000 people across the justice system.
projects.title: Civic Impact
projects.credits: Sonia Chokshi, Ian MacFarland, Allison Chan, William DeShazer

stories.title: Efficiency and dignity
stories.body:
During community supervision, individuals earn their way toward less intensive supervision or release by meeting court-mandated requirements over months or years. However, because progress lived across fragmented databases and paper files, officers spent hours manually compiling paperwork to verify eligibility. Staff often could not see who was already eligible, and even when they could, completing a change meant rebuilding the entire packet by hand. This created an administrative bottleneck where qualified people stayed stuck past the point they had earned their release, while officers lost hours to clerical work instead of supporting the people on their caseload.

We built an eligibility-to-action system that automatically identifies who qualifies for a change and pre-fills the required forms directly from their record. Working cross-functionally, we designed strict data validation rules that map directly to each state's source systems, eliminating manual data entry while preventing sync errors. This shifted the officer's role from data collector to reviewer, allowing staff to quickly review and file instead of starting from a blank packet.

We grounded the work in field-first research, designing alongside both Department of Corrections workers and the incarcerated population at each step of the process. In Tennessee, transfer packet completion times dropped from 30–60 minutes to a short review, saving officers over 1,000 hours shortly after launch.

stories.title: Access and agency
stories.body:
Another clear application of our dual strategy is our resident tablet product, designed to give incarcerated individuals direct visibility into their own trajectories. Inside facilities, essential information about sentence calculations, earned good time, and program eligibility traditionally lived behind staff barriers. Incarcerated people had to rely on case managers just to find out basic milestones, creating widespread anxiety, rumor-driven expectations, and endless administrative requests. Staff spent hours answering status questions rather than helping people prepare for release.

We spent time in facilities conducting field research, translating on-the-ground observations into clear product guardrails and a distinct, human-centered brand identity. The resulting interface translates dense policy and sentence calculations into plain language, showing people their exact timeline, earned credits, and upcoming eligibility dates. It introduces self-service features that allow residents to browse facility programming, bookmark courses, and complete key intake forms at their own pace, while intentionally excluding sensitive charge data to protect user privacy in shared living spaces.

As the product expanded to new state partners, we built out the design system infrastructure necessary to scale it sustainably. By establishing a unified foundation tailored for tablet environments, we ensured that state-specific variations could be deployed rapidly without compromising usability or brand integrity. Across partner states, over 60% of residents with access use the app monthly, while 80% of staff report a drop in repetitive sentence questions, proving how human-centered design and scalable systems can transform agency across an entire population.

stories.title: Clarity and trust
stories.body:
Beyond specific product workflows, designing for the criminal justice sector requires navigating an environment where trust is difficult to build and easy to lose. Traditional corrections software is either bleak legacy enterprise tech that treats people as line items, or overly polished corporate software that feels out of touch with the realities of incarceration. When standing up the design function, we needed a visual identity and voice that earned trust with state agency leadership while honoring the humanity of the people navigating the system. Aside from our company name, which usually takes people three tries to pronounce, we made sure every other part of our brand was unmistakable in its simplicity.

We built a brand and product language grounded in dignity, clarity, and utility. We established design principles that stripped away sensationalism and jargon in favor of plain language, transparent data visualization, and accessible interactions. We applied this ethos across every touchpoint, from our public-facing website and partnership proposals down to the daily software used on prison tablets and officer desktops. This cohesive identity established a distinct presence that resonated with both state leaders and frontline staff, helping position our platform as a trustworthy partner as we expanded nationwide.

projects.description:
Digital product and brand identity design for a wellness platform. Conceived as an iOS app, the audio-first anonymous community focused on mental health and emotional support.

Inline with its values, the harmful “endless feed” of information was omitted by design. The ephemeral content that took its place emphasized accessibility to marginalized people, especially the visually impaired. Service was supported for 2 years before shutting down in 2022.

workExperience.heading: Design at Independent
workExperience.description: Ran an independent design studio partnering with 11 select clients to launch new digital tools and brand identities from the ground up. Key work included designing an early-stage [mental health application](/p/a-emotional-health) that secured seed funding, building digital products for WeWork, creating an [election projections site](/p/a-election-consortium) for Princeton University, and laying the foundation for what later became [Recidiviz](/p/a-civic-impact). Additional projects included specialized software for [city planning](/p/a-city-planner), a platform for [dental operations](/p/a-dental-hygiene), and branding initiatives for organizations like [Schmidt Futures](/p/a-schmidt-futures).
workExperience.title: Design

workExperience.heading: Product at Google
workExperience.description: Led the end-to-end design of a [smart traffic application](/p/a-smart-cities) aimed at reducing city congestion by rewarding daily commuters for taking alternative transit routes. Guided the project through its full lifecycle, from early brainstorming and user research to final interface design and testing.
workExperience.title: Product

workExperience.heading: Growth at Google
workExperience.description: Shaped the products, campaigns, and external programs that helped scale [Waze](/p/a-waze) from 55 million to 110 million monthly active users. Established Waze’s first comprehensive brand standards manual, which laid the foundation for Pentagram’s later brand redesign. On the product side, designed user acquisition and onboarding flows for Waze Carpool and co-designed a self-serve platform for business partners to manage their presence. Also directed narrative video campaigns by selecting and managing external creative agencies.
workExperience.title: Growth

workExperience.heading: Product at Aerohive
workExperience.description: Elevated the user experience for enterprise [cloud-based networking software](/p/a-network-management) by transitioning the platform toward a mobile-first, map-centric interface. Partnered with the senior designer to overhaul the core monitoring dashboard, translating complex network health data into intuitive visual insights.
workExperience.title: Product

workExperience.heading: Research at GOTO Research
workExperience.description: Transformed complex behavioral research into clear visual narratives. Created detailed customer journey maps for major enterprise clients like Target to clarify user needs throughout the day and guide strategic business decisions.
workExperience.title: Research

workExperience.heading: Art Direction at Curran & Connors
workExperience.description: Led art direction and design for high-stakes [investor communications and annual reports](/p/a-various) for clients including FedEx, Activision Blizzard, and Chiquita. Directed photography, oversaw physical production details from paper selection to on-site press checks, and built out complementary digital experiences to extend each brand narrative online.
workExperience.title: Art Direction

workExperience.description: Made visual assets for early online communities, gaming forums, and social profiles.
workExperience.title: Graphic Design
